document_title: New fuel cell breakthrough could help power energy-hungry data centers

lessons.title: Why Data Centers Need New Power Sources
lessons.explanation: Data centers are multiplying across the United States, and they consume vast amounts of electricity. Power is needed not just to run the computing equipment but also to keep it cool. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates that data centers could account for as much as 9% of annual U.S. electricity generation by 2030, compared with 4% in 2023. This rapid growth puts pressure on the electric grid and motivates researchers to find alternative ways to generate electricity on-site. One promising option is the fuel cell, which can convert hydrogen and other fuels directly into electricity. Supplying electricity locally could reduce the burden placed on shared energy infrastructure.

lessons.title: How Fuel Cells Work
lessons.explanation: A fuel cell produces electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen. The process also generates water and heat. Catalysts help accelerate this reaction while limiting energy losses and supporting stronger performance and longer operating life. Designing the right catalyst remains a major challenge, because existing fuel cell catalysts still struggle to provide the combination of activity and durability needed to meet important performance goals. Understanding this basic chemistry is essential before exploring why platinum is the material of choice and why using less of it is so important.

lessons.title: The Platinum Tradeoff
lessons.explanation: Platinum is considered one of the most effective catalyst materials, but it is also a precious metal. Researchers therefore want to use as little platinum as possible without reducing effectiveness during energy conversion and storage. One way to stretch a small amount of platinum further is to turn it into nanoparticles, because breaking bulk platinum into extremely small particles dramatically increases the amount of surface exposed for chemical reactions. This makes it possible to use very small quantities of the metal, typically less than one quarter of a milligram per square centimeter. The problem is that platinum nanoparticles can change during fuel cell operation. They may dissolve, move to different locations, and grow larger, causing performance to gradually decline.

lessons.title: Why Ordered Intermetallic Catalysts Are Tricky
lessons.explanation: More recently, platinum intermetallic catalysts have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional platinum alloys because they can offer improved activity and stability. Producing them, however, involves another difficult compromise. To keep the nanoparticles small, evenly distributed and efficient in their use of platinum, researchers generally anneal the materials at temperatures below 700°C. Those temperatures are often too low to fully trigger the transition from a disordered atomic arrangement to a highly ordered one, which is important for maximizing both the activity and durability of intermetallic catalysts. There is a fundamental tension between achieving order and keeping particles small.
lessons.mermaid: graph TD; A[Low temperature anneal] --> B[Small, evenly distributed nanoparticles]; A --> C[Disordered atomic structure]; D[High temperature anneal] --> E[Ordered atomic structure]; D --> F[Particles clump together];

lessons.title: The Radial Nanochannel Carbon Solution
lessons.explanation: Wu and his colleagues developed a new carbon structure designed to overcome this limitation. The material consists of porous, hollow carbon spheres containing orderly radial nanochannels, along with substantial pore space and surface area. This structure allows large numbers of platinum cobalt intermetallic nanoparticles to remain densely packed yet evenly distributed. It also makes it possible to form the desired ordered intermetallic structure at much higher temperatures without causing the nanoparticles to clump together. Because of this special carbon nanostructured support, the team could heat the platinum-cobalt catalyst to 1000°C while still keeping nanoparticles smaller than 5 nanometers. In testing, the material retained 85% of its performance after 150,000 severe voltage cycles, corresponding to roughly 25,000 hours of operation. The open channel structure also helps ionomer spread evenly and makes it easier for protons, oxygen and water to move through the electrode.
